# moddio SDK

> Multiplayer games for modd.io. A game is a deterministic simulation (sim.ts) that runs on
> every player's machine and in the room, optional server hooks (server.ts), and a renderer in
> any engine (client/). Players send only typed inputs; the room orders them into frames, runs
> the sim as the authority and sends each frame's inputs to everyone. Your own inputs apply at
> once (prediction); the room corrects anyone who disagrees with it.

## Folder

    my-game/
      moddio.json   { "name": "my-game", "title": "My Game", "game": "<site slug>", "products": [...], "menu": true }
      sim.ts        export default defineSim({...})        the rules (players per room: its maxPlayers)
      server.ts     export default defineServer({...})     optional server-only hooks
      client/       index.html + main.ts                   the renderer (index.html loads main.js,
                                                           which is main.ts bundled by moddio dev/publish)
      assets/       images, sounds

Use relative paths for every file a game loads: `main.js`, `assets/hero.png`, `client/style.css`,
never `/main.js` or `/assets/...`. A published game may be served under a path (on a preview or
behind a proxy, at /__g/<version>--<game>/), where a path starting with / points outside it.
`moddio dev` and the site serve the same files at the same relative paths.

Start: `npx moddio@latest create my-game --template blank|arena|soccer|legacy|marble [--game <slug>]`, then
`cd my-game && npm install`. The SDK is one npm package, moddio (`npm i -D moddio` in a folder of your own):
it carries @moddio/sim, @moddio/server and @moddio/client, and its CLI resolves those imports.
Commands: `moddio dev` (local room + page; open ?player=a and ?player=b, or
/__moddio/play?player=a for the play page's sandboxed frame), `moddio test` (run after every
change; `moddio engines` once adds JavaScriptCore and SpiderMonkey to it), `moddio play` (the
game in headless Chromium with scripted input: screenshots and console logs; see Testing),
`moddio login`, `moddio publish`. Outputs go under the project's .moddio/.

npm packages: `moddio add <name>[@version]` (`moddio remove <name>`), not `npm install`. Only
packages from the npm registry (no git, URLs or files). They go in the game's npm/ folder:
npm/package.json and npm/package-lock.json belong to the game; npm/node_modules is installed again
from them by the next build when missing. Import them as usual from sim.ts, server.ts or client/;
the bundles carry them to players, so prefer small, well-known packages. The sim must stay
deterministic with them too (no Math.random, Date or timers inside): `moddio test` checks.

## sim.ts

    import { defineSim } from '@moddio/sim';

    export default defineSim({
      name: 'my-game',             // short id
      version: '1',                // bump when the rules change
      tickRate: 20,                // ticks per second (default 20)
      maxPlayers: 16,
      input: { move: ['i8', 'i8'], aim: 'u16', buttons: { flags: ['fire', 'jump'] } },  // the input SHAPE

      init(ctx) { return { players: {}, coins: [] }; },            // starting state; ctx.rng, ctx.seed, ctx.config
      join(state, id, ctx, info) {     // info: { id, name, avatar, roles } from the player's ticket
        state.players[id] = { name: info.name, x: 0, y: 0, move: [0, 0], fire: false };
      },
      leave(state, id, ctx) { delete state.players[id]; },
      disconnect(state, id, ctx) {},   // optional: connection lost, seat kept (default: nothing)
      reconnect(state, id, ctx) {},    // optional
      onInput(state, id, input, ctx) { // the player's latest input; store it, act in step
        const p = state.players[id];
        p.move = [input.move[0] / 128, input.move[1] / 128];
        p.fire = input.buttons.fire;
      },
      event(state, e, ctx) {},         // a server event (from server.ts), on its frame
      predict: 'self',                 // the default; or 'world' (see Prediction below)
      step(state, ctx) {               // one tick
        for (const id of Object.keys(state.players).sort()) {
          const p = state.players[id];
          p.x += p.move[0] * 5; p.y += p.move[1] * 5;
        }
      },
    });

### Input shapes

Scalars: `i8 u8 i16 u16 i32 u32 f32 bool`. Tuples: `['i8', 'i8']` (arrays). Bitfields:
`{ flags: ['fire', 'jump'] }` (an object of booleans, up to 32). A record of fields is the
top level. At most 64 bytes. Values are clamped and truncated to their type (f32 rounded,
non-finite becomes 0); the room drops any input that is not exactly the shape.

An input HOLDS until the next one: the client sends inputs only when they change. So store
the latest input in the state in onInput and act on it in step; never treat an input as
"this tick only".

### ctx

    ctx.frame       ticks since the room began (seconds = frame / tickRate)
    ctx.tickRate
    ctx.rng()       [0, 1), deterministic: the same on every client
    ctx.int(n)      integer in [0, n)
    ctx.players     player ids in the room, sorted
    ctx.out(effect) ask the platform for something: { save: data, player }, { offer: 'sword', player }
                    (the purchase dialog, see Shop), { purchase, accept } (the answer to a
                    `purchased` event, see Shop), { text: 'ask', player }. Every client computes
                    effects; only the room's are carried out.
    ctx.physics     the physics world, if the sim declares `physics`
    ctx.config      (init only) the room's settings

### Rules (the realm enforces them; the errors say what to use)

- No Math.random (use ctx.rng), no Date or timers (count ctx.frame), no fetch/WebSocket (use
  ctx.out and server events), no Intl/toLocaleString/localeCompare (compare with < and >).
  These do not exist in the sim: it runs in its own realm with them removed.
- Math.sin/cos/tan/exp/log/pow/atan2/hypot/cbrt... are deterministic replacements, the same bits
  in every browser. `**` is compiled to the same Math.pow. + - * / and Math.sqrt are exact.
- State is plain data: objects, arrays, numbers, strings, booleans, null (and Uint8Array). No
  classes, Map, Set, Date, functions, and no object referenced from two places (store ids).
- Iterate players in a fixed order: `Object.keys(state.players).sort()`.
- Never branch on anything but the state, the input and ctx.
- Secrets cannot live in the sim (every client has the whole state): hidden randomness comes
  from the server as an event when it happens.

### Physics

Rapier (deterministic build), 2D or 3D:

    import RAPIER from '@dimforge/rapier2d-deterministic-compat';
    import { rapier, bodyFingerprint, renderBodies } from '@moddio/sim/rapier';
    defineSim({ physics: rapier(RAPIER, { gravity: { x: 0, y: 0 }, timestep: 1 / 20 }),
      init(ctx) { const world = ctx.physics; ... },        // typed: RAPIER.World, no casts
      step(state, ctx) { ... ctx.physics.step(); },
      fingerprint: (state, id, { physics }) => bodyFingerprint(physics, state.players[id].body),
      render: (state, { physics }) => ({ ...state, bodies: renderBodies(physics) }) })

Keep body HANDLES (numbers) in the state; get bodies with `ctx.physics.getRigidBody(handle)`.
`bodyFingerprint(world, handle)` is a body's pose to the centimetre (the usual 'self'
fingerprint); `renderBodies(world)` lists every collider as plain data for render():
`{ h, x, y, a, r }` (ball) or `{ h, x, y, a, hx, hy }` (box) in 2D; `z`, quaternion `q` and box
half extents `e` in 3D. `h` is the body handle.

Planck.js 0.3.22 (moddio2's physics):

    import { planck, pl } from '@moddio/sim/planck';
    defineSim({ physics: planck({ gravity: { x: 0, y: 0 } }),
      init(ctx) { const world = ctx.physics; const b = world.createBody({ type: 'dynamic', position: pl.Vec2(1, 2) });
                  b.createFixture(pl.Circle(0.5), { density: 1 }); return { ball: world.idOf(b) }; },
      step(state, ctx) { const world = ctx.physics; world.step(1 / 20, 8, 3);
                         for (const c of world.contacts()) { /* { type: 'begin'|'end', a, b, sensor } by body id */ } } })

Keep body ids (`world.idOf(body)`) in the state; look up with `world.bodyOf(id)`. Read contacts
with `world.contacts()` right after `world.step()`. Contact listeners you add yourself must be
registered in `planck({ setup(world, pl) { ... } })`, which runs on every rebuilt world.
With the default `predict: 'self'`, a physics game returns its own body's pose from
`fingerprint(state, id, { physics })`, rounded to centimetres (see Prediction).

### Any other physics library: write a driver

Games may use any physics library, as long as it is deterministic. `moddio test` proves it:
the sim must hash the same in V8, JavaScriptCore and SpiderMonkey every tick, or the game
doesn't publish. Plug a library in with a `PhysicsDriver` (exported by `@moddio/sim`):

    const myPhysics: PhysicsDriver<MyWorld> = {
      kind: 'mylib',
      canonicalEvery: 0,          // 0 if save/load is exact; else rebuild every N frames (below)
      predict: 'self',            // optional: the default prediction mode for games on it
      async ready() { /* load wasm etc. once */ },
      create() { return new MyWorld(); },                 // a fresh world, for init
      save(world) { return /* plain data: everything load needs */; },
      load(data) { return /* a world that continues exactly like the saved one */; },
      digest(world, h, q) { return /* fold every body's state into hash h; round numbers to 1/q when q is given */; },
      free(world) { /* release wasm memory; called when a world is abandoned */ },
      view(world) { return world; },                     // optional: what the game sees as ctx.physics
    };
    defineSim({ physics: myPhysics, ... })

When each is called:
- `create`: once per room, before `init`.
- `save`: for snapshots (joiners, corrections) and when the prediction is copied.
- `load`: when a client joins mid-game, is corrected, or rolls back. It must be a pure function
  of what `save` returned.
- `digest`: every frame for the room's hash and the cross-engine check; with `q`, for the
  prediction's fingerprint.

**Exact or canonical.** If a world restored with `load(save(w))` steps bit-for-bit like `w`,
set `canonicalEvery: 0` (Rapier, Box2dWeb with care). If it doesn't (a library whose contact
cache or broad-phase tree is history, not data, like Planck), set `canonicalEvery` (e.g. 100):
every world, the room's included, is rebuilt from its own save on those frames, so all of them
agree again by construction, and snapshots are taken only on those frames.

**Pitfall: state outside the world.** Some libraries keep settings in module- or class-level
variables that only their world constructor sets (Box2dWeb does this for two settings). A
client restored with `load` never runs that constructor, so it silently drifts from the room
and keeps being corrected. `load` must set every such global itself. Node tests can't show
this, because there the room and the clients share one realm; the browser test can.

### Prediction

Your own player always has zero input delay. The default, `predict: 'self'`, predicts only your
player: the renderer draws everyone else from the room's world, interpolated (smooth, about a
playout delay behind), and itself from `self` (see client). Physics games return their own
body's pose from `fingerprint(state, id, { physics })`, rounded to centimetres (used only in
'self' mode; 'world' always compares the whole world).

Choose `predict: 'world'` only when the local player's actions on others must show at once -
shoving another player's body, grabbing a shared item first, a melee hit that must land on
screen the instant you press. The whole predicted world is then kept in step with the room and
drawn as one (`state` and `self` are the same world); remote players can snap when the room
corrects them, and it costs more CPU (a rebuild on about 40% of ticks, against 1%).

## server.ts

    import { defineServer } from '@moddio/server';

    export default defineServer({
      async join(player, room) {           // player: { id, name, roles }
        room.event({ type: 'loaded', id: player.id, save: await room.save.get(player) });
      },
      async leave(player, room) {},
      async effect(effect, room) {         // the room's ctx.out effects
        if ('save' in effect) await room.save.set(effect.player, effect.save);
      },
      tick(room) {                         // every frame; may be async (skipped while still running)
        if (room.frame % 600 === 0 && room.random() < 0.5) room.event({ type: 'boss', x: room.random() * 100 });
      },
    });

room: `id` (the room's name), `state` (a per-room object for anything the hooks keep),
`event(e)` (plain data; returns the frame it applies on, a few frames ahead, the same frame for
everyone), `private(player, data)` (to one player, outside the state; each event or private message
at most 64 KB as JSON, 32 of them a frame), `save.get/set` (64 KB per
player), `shop.purchases(player)` (see Shop), `random()`, `frame`, `players`, `log()`.
Hooks never change the state directly: only through room.event.

Every `ctx.out({...})` the sim makes, whatever its shape, reaches `effect` (from the room's own
copy of the sim only). The hooks run in a sandbox, one per room: no require, process, fs, fetch
or timers, a CPU limit per call (a hook stuck in a loop is stopped, and the room plays on), and
module-level variables are per room. `moddio test` runs them that way and reports which hooks
ran, which events they inserted, and fails if any hook threw.

## client (renderer)

    import { playInWorker, canvas2d, controls, mergeSelf } from '@moddio/client/browser';

    const view = canvas2d(canvas);       // sized to the window at screen density, resized only when it is
    const keys = controls(canvas);
    const game = await playInWorker({
      input: () => ({ move: keys.move().map((v) => v * 127), aim: 0, buttons: { fire: keys.mouse.down, jump: keys.pressed(' ') } }),
    });
    game.onFrame(({ state, self }) => {  // every screen frame, interpolated
      const ctx = view.begin('#101418'); // transform reset to CSS pixels, background filled
      const s = mergeSelf(state, self, 'players', game.player);   // everyone from state, you from self
      if (s) draw(ctx, s, view.width, view.height);
    });
    game.onEffect((effect, frame) => {});    // confirmed effects
    game.onPrivate((data) => {});
    game.player                              // your player id

The sim, the netcode and the room connection run in a Web Worker; the page samples `input`
continuously and draws. What onFrame hands over is the sim's `render(state, { physics })`
output (or its state, if it has no render), interpolated between the two ticks around this
instant (numbers blended, objects by key, arrays by item `id`/`h`): `state` is what to draw,
`self` the local player's world at its own clock: draw everyone from `state` and yourself from
`self` (in predict 'world' they are the same world). `mergeSelf(state, self, 'players', id)` does
that for a record keyed by player id; for an array, name the item key:
`mergeSelf(state, self, 'bodies', state.players[me].body, 'h')`.

`controls(canvas)`: `keys` (held, lower-case `KeyboardEvent.key`), `move()` (WASD/arrows as
[-1..1, -1..1]), `mouse` ({ x, y } in CSS pixels, `down`, `buttons` [main, middle, secondary];
no context menu over the canvas), `pressed(key)` (true once per press of a key or 'mouse0'..'mouse2',
for one-shot actions), `world({ scale, ox, oy })` (the pointer in world units, given screen =
world * scale + offset), `touch` (the player is on a phone or tablet).

Players also play on phones and tablets, so every game must be playable by touch. `controls`
reads touch for you: a finger on the left half of the canvas drags an on-screen stick that
`move()` returns (once the game calls move()); any other finger is the mouse (position, `down`, a
'mouse0' press). Every other key the game uses needs an on-screen button:
`controls(canvas, { buttons: [{ key: ' ', label: 'Jump' }, { key: 'e', label: 'Use' }] })` shows
them at the bottom right on touch screens only; holding one holds its key (and fires keydown/keyup,
so a game's own key listeners see it too). Keep the HUD clear of
the bottom corners on touch screens, and readable on a small screen (`view.width` may be 360). `canvas2d(canvas, { size: 'element', hiDpi: false })` follows the
element's CSS size or draws one canvas pixel per CSS pixel; `view.onResize(cb)`. A physics game must define `render` and return its bodies'
poses as plain data: the physics world lives in the worker, out of the page's reach.

    render(state, { physics }) { return { players: state.players, bodies: [/* { x, y, angle, ... } */] }; }

On the play page, the client asks the page for a ticket (postMessage), which names the room,
the player and the room host; under `moddio dev` it uses room '<game>/dev', ?player= from the
URL, and this page's host. Pages are served as the site serves them: sandboxed (opaque origin),
no eval, no inline scripts, no localStorage or cookies, no other hosts, no WebRTC, no frames of its own (a
srcdoc frame or a data:/blob: page runs none of the game's scripts). /__moddio/play?player=a
stands in for the play page. Load scripts with type="module".

Your inputs apply at once (zero input delay). Never change the state in the renderer.

### Servers (the game's own menu)

The play page has no lobby: the server list, joining a friend's server and starting a new one
are the game's to show, in its own menu drawn by the client. A game starts one of two ways:

- Straight into a server (the default): opening the game puts the player in the best open
  server running the game's current version (or a new one), and the play page shows that
  server's player list and chat beside it. Give the game a menu (a button or a key, e.g. Esc)
  with at least a server list, to switch with `switchRoom`.
- At its own menu, in no server (`"menu": true` in moddio.json): for a game whose first screen is
  a title or main menu with Play, a server picker, a character or skin choice. The player isn't in
  any server: nobody sees them, no seat is taken, and the play page shows no player list or chat
  until they join one from the menu. A link or invite to a server, a reload while in one, and
  switchRoom still start in that server, so always check where the game starts:

    import { atMenu, joinRoom, leaveRoom, playInWorker } from '@moddio/client/browser';

    if (await atMenu()) {            // true: at the menu, in no server; false: a server is waiting
      await showMenu();              // the menu ends when the player picks and joinRoom resolves:
      //   await joinRoom();                         Play: what the site's Play does (the fullest
      //                                              server with space in the player's region, else a new one)
      //   await joinRoom(r.name);                   a server from pageRooms()
      //   await joinRoom('region', { region: 'eu' }); joinRoom('new', { region: 'eu' })
    }
    const game = await playInWorker({ input: ... });   // connects to the server joined
    // later, "Main menu" (after a round, from a pause menu):
    await leaveRoom();               // stops `game` (the room sees the player leave), back at no server
    await showMenu();                // and in again: joinRoom(...), then playInWorker(...)

  At the menu there is no state: the client draws the menu from its own assets (a title screen,
  the map, a preview of the player's character), not from onFrame. pageRooms() works there
  (`current` is null). joinRoom keeps the game loaded, so what the menu set up stays (a picked
  skin, a name: send it as input or with the first frames, since the sim knows nothing of the
  menu). It rejects with the reason when it can't (full, closed, not allowed): show it and stay at
  the menu. A server on another version of the game (an older one still open) and watching
  (`{ watch: true }`) load the game again in that server instead: atMenu() is false then. Calling
  playInWorker at the menu without joinRoom does quick play. buy() needs a server (the sim accepts
  each purchase), so a shop on the menu joins first, or sells once in game. Under `moddio dev`,
  /__moddio/play opens at the menu too, and every server the menu names is the one dev room.

Either way, the server list:

    import { pageRooms, switchRoom } from '@moddio/client/browser';

    const { current, region, regions, rooms } = await pageRooms();
    // current: the server this game is in (null at the menu). region: the player's nearest ('na' | 'sa' | 'eu' | 'asia').
    // regions: every region a server can open in, in display order, even ones with no server:
    //   [{ id: 'na', name: 'North America' }, { id: 'sa', name: 'South America' },
    //    { id: 'eu', name: 'Europe' }, { id: 'asia', name: 'Asia' }]
    // rooms: [{ name, label, players, maxPlayers, versionLabel, full, spectators, region, colo }]
    for (const g of regions) {
      const here = rooms.filter((r) => r.region === g.id);
      header(g.name, g.id === region ? 'nearest' : '');
      here.forEach((r, i) => row(`${g.name} ${i + 1}`, `${r.players}/${r.maxPlayers}`,   // "Asia 1", "Asia 2"
        r.name === current ? 'here' : r.full ? 'full' : 'join'));
      if (!here.length) row(`${g.name} 1`, '0 players', 'start');                    // an empty region
    }
    switchRoom(r.name, { onFailed: (why) => toast(why) });   // join that server
    switchRoom('region', { region: 'asia' });                // join Asia: its fullest server with space, else a new one there
    switchRoom('new', { region: 'asia' });                   // always a new server, in Asia
    switchRoom('new');                                        // a new server, in the player's nearest region
    switchRoom(r.name, { watch: true });                      // spectate (when r.spectators)

pageRooms reads the list fresh each call (ask again when the menu opens; don't poll faster than
every few seconds). From the menu, join with joinRoom (it keeps the game loaded); in a server,
move with switchRoom. switchRoom reloads the game's frame in the other server: the game starts
again there with a new ticket, like a fresh load. Nothing in memory survives; what should carry
over belongs in the sim's state or server.ts. A server keeps the version it started on, so the
list can show older versions; label them with versionLabel. The page allows one switch every
2 s (joins and switches together), and a refused switch (full, closed, not allowed) leaves the
player where they are and calls onFailed.

Regions: every server runs in one of North America ('na'), South America ('sa'), Europe ('eu')
or Asia ('asia'), and reports it as `region`. Build the region list from pageRooms' `regions`
(don't hard-code it), number servers within their region by their order in `rooms` ("Asia 1",
"Asia 2"), and don't show server ids or version strings as names. Play (the site's button, and
joinRoom() with no server named) puts a player in the fullest server with space in their nearest
region, else starts one there; it never puts them in another region. `colo` is the data centre a server runs in (an airport code
such as "HKG", "AMS", "IAD"): for debugging, not for labels. South American servers run in the
eastern US for now (Cloudflare, which hosts them, has no data centre for game servers in South
America); they still show as South America. `regions` is [] and every `region` null when the
game's servers don't run by region (games on the dedicated heavy host). Under `moddio dev` the
list is the one dev room (region null) with the four regions, and switching is refused.

Inspection, for tests, HUDs and the console: `game.inspect()` returns `{ confirmed: { frame,
state }, predicted: { frame, state }, hashAt(frame), stats, report, mode }`; `report.desync`
counts the room's hash checks (agreed / disagreed). For a ping on a HUD use `report.pingMs` (the
network round trip to the room, null until known), not the gap between the predicted and confirmed
frames: that gap is the prediction lead, which also holds the tick an input is aimed at and a
jitter margin, and reads around 80 ms over the real ping at 30 Hz. `report.leadMs` is that lead
in ms and `report.marginMs` its safety margin (both null with `inputLead: false`).
`game.frameView()` returns what onFrame would draw now. A browser game is also on `window.moddioGame`.

Input lead: by default each input is aimed at a frame a lead ahead (a round trip plus a safety
margin that grows after a late input) and the room holds it until then; that is what prediction
needs. A game that draws its own player from the room's state (no prediction) should pass
`inputLead: false` to `playInWorker` / `play`: each input is then sent the moment it changes and the
room applies it on its next tick, so the delay is one trip there, at most a tick, and one trip back.

Spectators: `watch({ sim, url, room })` (from '@moddio/client') runs the sim on the room's
ticks and sends nothing that counts. `{ text: 'ask' }` and `{ offer }` effects
for your player are shown by the play page; the answer comes back as a server event.

Headless (Node, bots, tests): `import { play } from '@moddio/client'` runs Lockstep in-process
with a sim loaded by `loadSimFile` from '@moddio/sim/node'.

## Shop

Players buy a game's products with their modd.io tokens; the game's creator gets 90% of each
sale. What a product *is* (an item, a skin, a unit, a potion, an unlock) is entirely the game's
business: the platform only knows its id, name, price and whether it sells once.

### 1. List what is for sale (moddio.json)

    "products": [
      { "id": "potion", "name": "Health Potion", "price": 30 },
      { "id": "gold-skin", "name": "Gold Skin", "price": 400, "once": true,
        "description": "Shiny.", "image": "assets/skins/gold.png" }
    ]

Prices are whole tokens, 1 to 1,000,000; at most 500 products. `once: true`: a player buys it
at most once and owns it for good (skins, unlocks); without it, as often as they like (potions,
ammo). `image` is a file under assets/. The published moddio.json is the only price list: the
game names a product by id and never sets a price.

### 2. Sell it (client or sim)

    import { buy } from '@moddio/client/browser';
    const r = await buy('potion');   // { ok: true, purchase, balance } | { ok: false, cancelled, error }

or from the sim: ctx.out({ offer: 'potion', player }). The game draws its own shop however it
likes; buy() opens modd.io's purchase dialog, outside the game's frame, with the name and price
from moddio.json. Only the player's click there buys. buy() resolves once it is all done:
`ok: true` means the player paid *and the game took the item*; a decline resolves
`{ ok: false, error }` with the game's reason. Use the result only for the game's UI (close the
shop, say thanks). Never grant anything from it.

### 3. Give it, and answer (sim)

The item arrives as a server event on a frame every client applies:
{ type: 'purchased', player, product, purchase, price }. Answer it in the same event() call:

    event(state, e, ctx) {
      if (e.type !== 'purchased') return;
      const p = state.players[e.player];
      if (!p) return ctx.out({ purchase: e.purchase, accept: false, reason: 'You are not in the game' });
      if (e.product === 'potion') {
        if (p.bag.length >= 20) return ctx.out({ purchase: e.purchase, accept: false, reason: 'Your bag is full' });
        p.bag.push('potion');
      } else if (e.product === 'gold-skin') {
        p.skins.push('gold'); p.skin = 'gold';       // owned and worn at once
      } else {
        return ctx.out({ purchase: e.purchase, accept: false, reason: 'Not sold here any more' });
      }
      ctx.out({ purchase: e.purchase, accept: true });
    }

- Accept once the item is the player's: granted, equipped, whatever the game does with it.
- Decline when it can't be given (a full bag, a unit that can't hold it, a product the game no
  longer has). `reason` is shown to the player in the purchase dialog; keep it short.
- The player is charged only for an accept. A decline, or no answer on that frame, gives the
  tokens back, and the creator gets nothing. So answer every `purchased` event, on its frame:
  not later, not from the client, not from server.ts. `moddio test` buys each product once and
  fails if any goes unanswered.
- Only the room's copy of the sim counts (it is authoritative), so a client can't fake an answer
  or an item. The same purchase never arrives twice.

The types are in @moddio/sim: `PurchasedEvent` and `PurchaseAnswer`.

### 4. Keep what was bought `once` (server.ts)

Things bought `once` belong to the player even if a save is lost: grant them again on join.
room.shop.purchases(player) lists what the player bought and the game took (newest first,
declined and refunded ones left out):

    async join(player, room) {
      const owned = (await room.shop.purchases(player)).filter((p) => p.once).map((p) => p.product);
      room.event({ type: 'owned', player: player.id, products: owned });   // the sim grants these
    }

Things bought as often as players like (potions) are the game's to keep: put them in the save.

Prices in the game's own currency (gold, points) are game rules: the sim checks and takes them.
Under `moddio dev`, open /__moddio/play?player=a: buying asks with confirm(), pays nothing, and
goes through the same answer (the terminal says when the game declined or didn't answer).

## Invites

Players invite friends with the Invite button beside the game. Its link is one short code
(modd.io/i/x1j3b) that opens the game straight into the inviter's room (server) and, when the
inviter is signed in, names them. When a friend who came
through a player's invite link to this game makes a modd.io account and plays for a while, modd.io
gives both of them tokens, and the game gets a server event in the inviter's room:

    { type: 'invited', player, friend }     // player: the inviter; friend: the friend's id in this game

It arrives once per friend, while the inviter is in one of the game's rooms (the next time they
are, if they aren't now). The friend may be elsewhere. Give the inviter something in the sim to
thank them (a skin, an item, coins), and keep it in their save (server.ts) like anything else they
own:

    event(state, e, ctx) {
      if (e.type !== 'invited') return;
      const p = state.players[e.player];
      if (p) p.skins.push('friend-badge');
    }

Nothing needs answering. The type is in @moddio/sim: `InvitedEvent`.

Don't make the game's own invite links, codes or "who invited you?" questions: the game never sees
the page's address, so a code in a link can't reach it, and modd.io already checks that each friend
is a real new player (a new account, a verified email, play time the room host measured) before
the event comes. To get players inviting, point them at the Invite button and reward the event.

## Chat and speech bubbles

The room's chat is modd.io's, beside the game (Enter opens it). The game can show its messages,
for example as speech bubbles over the sender:

    import { onChat } from '@moddio/client/browser';
    onChat((m) => {               // { id, player, name, text }, each new message as it arrives
      bubbles.set(m.player, { text: m.text, until: performance.now() + 5000 });
    });
    // in draw(): for each live bubble, find the entity whose player id is m.player
    // (the same "p_..." id the sim uses) and draw m.text above it

The text is already filtered (no links or slurs, swear words starred out), and messages from
players this player muted never arrive. Messages come to each browser, not through the sim:
use them for what the player sees, never for game rules or state. The game can't send chat.
Under `moddio dev`, the play page stand-in has a chat box at the top right (Enter in the game
focuses it); it reaches every dev tab of the room, and window.moddioChat(text, player?) sends one
from a script.

## Publishing

`moddio login` (once; the site shows a code to allow), then `moddio publish`: it builds, runs
`moddio test` on the same bundle, writes it (sim.js, server.js, client/, assets/ under their
own paths, manifest.json) and uploads it as a new version, together with the game folder's
source (everything but node_modules, .moddio/, dist/, .git, .env files and keys, and what the
folder's own .gitignore leaves out), so the game can be changed with AI and copied on modd.io.
The game's slug is recorded in moddio.json ("game"). `--public` makes the game playable by anyone with the link once the
version passes review. `--local` only writes the bundle. MODDIO_SITE and MODDIO_TOKEN override the site and
the token.

## Testing

`moddio test` plays the game with bots (random inputs of your shape, joiners, dropped
connections, lossy links) and checks that every client's state hash equals the room's on every
frame; replays the round in V8, JavaScriptCore and SpiderMonkey and checks every tick's hash;
and reports CPU per tick and per rollback, state size and bandwidth. With a shop, one bot
buys every product once mid-match: each `purchased` event must be answered on its frame. A mismatch means the sim
is not deterministic: look for randomness or time, iteration order that depends on history,
or state kept outside the state object (module-level variables).

`moddio play` shows what players see: the game served as on modd.io (its CSP, the play page's
sandboxed frame) in headless Chromium, 1 to 4 players (`--players`), for `--seconds` of play
(default 10, at most 120, counted once everyone joined). Each player can follow a script of
steps (`--script`, JSON or a file: one array for every player, or an array of arrays):
`{"wait":ms}`, `{"down":"d"}`, `{"up":"d"}`, `{"press":"Space"}`, `{"type":"text"}`,
`{"move":[x,y]}`, `{"click":[x,y],"button":"left"}`, `{"mousedown":[x,y]}`, `{"mouseup":[x,y]}`,
`{"shot":"label"}`; x,y are CSS pixels in the 960x600 game frame. `--shots 2,5` adds screenshots
at those seconds; one is taken at the end. It writes .moddio/play/<run>/: p1-<label>.png, p1-console.log
(console, uncaught errors, workers), room.log and summary.json, and prints the paths, frames,
errors, and anything the game tried to reach outside its files and room (refused, as on modd.io).

    npx moddio play --players 2 --seconds 8 --shots 3 --script '[[{"down":"d"},{"wait":2000},{"up":"d"},{"click":[480,300]}],[]]'
